```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="k01" data-src="../assets/learn/data/town.json ../assets/learn/data/town_year.json ../assets/learn/data/town_days.json ../assets/learn/data/01-power-energy.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Units and powers of ten, in six moves</p>
<ol>
<li>Each prefix is 1,000 times the one below: Prairie Town's demand is scaled so its busiest hour of 2025 is 450 MW, which is 450,000 kW or 0.45 GW.</li>
<li>Energy is power × time: on 3 September 2025 the town's 24 hourly values add up to 6,957 MWh, or 6.957 GWh.</li>
<li>Units cancel like numbers: at a flat $40/MWh, 1,965 MWh × $40/MWh = $78,600; and 6,957 MWh ÷ 24 h ≈ 289.9 MW, the day's average power.</li>
<li>Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, with a at least 1 and less than 10: 1,000 = 10³, and the day's 6,957,000,000 Wh ≈ 6.96 × 10⁹ Wh.</li>
<li>Written in Wh as powers of ten, a phone charge (1.9 × 10¹) and the U.S. year (4.2 × 10¹⁵) are 14 powers of ten apart.</li>
<li>The day lies between 235 MW × 24 h = 5,640 MWh and 353 MW × 24 h = 8,472 MWh, so a report of 6,957 GWh has a slipped prefix.</li>
</ol>
<div class="k1-tables">

<tr><td>Charging a smartphone once</td><td>0.019 kWh</td><td class="k1-wh">19</td><td>1.9 × 10¹ Wh</td></tr>

<tr><td>Prairie Town's day, 3 September 2025</td><td>6,957 MWh</td><td class="k1-wh">6,957,000,000</td><td>6.96 × 10⁹ Wh</td></tr>
<tr><td>The Southwest Power Pool's year, 2025</td><td>298.6 TWh</td><td class="k1-wh">298,600,000,000,000</td><td>2.99 × 10¹⁴ Wh</td></tr>
<tr><td>The United States' year, 2025</td><td>about 4,200 TWh</td><td class="k1-wh">4,200,000,000,000,000</td><td>4.2 × 10¹⁵ Wh</td></tr>
</tbody></table>

<li><b>Source.</b> Prairie Town's day is the real hourly demand shape of 3 September 2025 on the Southwest Power Pool grid (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a>).</li>
<li><b>Illustrative.</b> Scaled as in <a href="00-grid-operator.html">lesson 0</a>: 450 MW in 2025's busiest hour, before lesson 0's rounding (at most 2.5 MW an hour). The town, its scale and the flat $40/MWh gas running cost are illustrative.</li>
<li><b>Not a schedule.</b> $78,600 prices all 1,965 MWh of gas at one flat $40/MWh. Lesson 0's schedule, held to ramp limits, runs 1,960 MWh at $40/MWh and 20 MWh on a $100/MWh peak plant: $80,400.</li>
```

::: {#explain .lx-sec}

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="k1-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Prefix</dt><dd>A letter that multiplies a unit: k by 1,000, M by a million, G by a billion, T by a trillion.</dd>
<dt>Power and energy</dt><dd>Power (MW) is a rate; energy (MWh) is power held over time: MW × h = MWh.</dd>
<dt>Units cancel</dt><dd>A unit on top cancels the same unit underneath: $/MWh × MWh leaves $.</dd>
<dt>Scientific notation</dt><dd>A number at least 1 and less than 10, times a power of ten: the town's day is about 6.96 × 10⁹ Wh.</dd>
<dt>Order-of-magnitude check</dt><dd>Bound a number from both sides; missing by a power of ten points to a slipped prefix or unit.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Exponents, logarithms and the joule</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Multiply: add the exponents.** $10^3 \times 10^6 = 10^9$: a thousand MW is a GW.
- **Divide: subtract them.** $\dfrac{4.2 \times 10^{15}}{1.9 \times 10^{1}} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{14}$: the U.S. year in phone charges.
- **The logarithm is the exponent.** $\log_{10}(6.96 \times 10^9) \approx 9.84$. A [log scale]{.lx-term term="log-scale"} spaces 1, 10 and 100 Wh evenly, so one chart holds a phone and a nation.
- **The joule.** A watt is one joule per second, so 1 Wh = 3,600 J and 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ, exactly. Heat units such as the MMBtu come in [toolbox K2](k02-rates-efficiencies.html).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Units inside a model (a preview)</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Choose units that keep numbers modest.** Models write MW and \$/MWh, not W and \$/Wh, so their coefficients (the fixed numbers in front of each unknown) are not needlessly far apart in size. Sensible units help a [solver]{.lx-term term="solver"}; they do not guarantee a well-scaled model.
- **Put the unit in the name.** `demand_mw * hours` is MWh and `gas_mwh * price_usd_per_mwh` is dollars. Terms added together must share a unit: MW plus MW, never MW plus MWh.
- **Where next.** Bridge [B3](b03-read-check-formulation.html) checks that every term of a model's balance has one unit; [M1](m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html) builds a dispatch model in MW and \$/MWh. Checking a model's numerical scaling belongs to those lessons.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="k1-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="kwh" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A kWh is a kilowatt per hour.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A kWh is kilowatts × hours: energy. “Per hour” is how fast something changes, like lesson 0's <span class="lx-term" data-term="ramp-rate">ramp limit</span> of 40 MW per hour.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="bigger" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “450 MW is more power than 0.45 GW.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. They are the same power: a bigger unit takes a smaller number.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="k1">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spp" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">The Southwest Power Pool's demand in 2025 was 298.6 TWh. How many GWh is that?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">0.2986 GWh</li><li data-value="b">298,600 GWh</li><li data-value="c">298,600,000 GWh</li><li data-value="d">2,986 GWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>298,600 GWh: a TWh is 1,000 GWh, and a smaller unit takes a bigger number. 298,600,000 is the same energy in MWh.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="apart" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">About how many powers of ten from the electricity an average U.S. home buys in a year (1.08 × 10⁷ Wh) to the Southwest Power Pool's year (2.99 × 10¹⁴ Wh)?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">5</li><li data-value="b">7</li><li data-value="c">14</li><li data-value="d">21</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>7. Exponents: 14 − 7 = 7. Leading numbers: 2.99 ÷ 1.08 ≈ 2.8. So the ratio is about 2.8 × 10⁷.</p><p>2.8 is below 3.16 (√10, the midpoint of 1 and 10 on a log scale), so the nearest power stays 10⁷.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="k1-drill"></div>
```
